text: With the foundational decision made, it's time to turn it into real design work: domain structure, integrations, and security, for the same organization.

Check Meridian against Chapter 2's actual test for Domain Separation: separate subsidiaries under one parent, or an MSP's distinct clients. St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View match the first case exactly — their day-to-day incidents and HR cases genuinely shouldn't cross, but Meridian's corporate leadership needs one combined view for board reporting. So the design is one instance, three domains, one Meridian corporate domain on top. The real cost — every script and integration now has to be domain-aware — is accepted because this separation need is genuinely structural, not a generic department split.

Next, the HR integration. Migrating Workday, ADP, and Prairie View's homegrown PeopleSoft module onto one system inside eighteen months isn't realistic. So ServiceNow HR Service Delivery becomes the system of engagement, while each legacy platform stays the system of record for now: an IntegrationHub spoke for Workday, a custom Scripted REST integration for ADP, and a MID Server pulling scheduled extracts for Prairie View's API-less on-prem system. All three go into the integration inventory with named owners before any code gets written.

Not every piece of that integration uses the same pattern. A new-hire record syncing in from Workday doesn't need an immediate answer, so it's event-driven — publish the event, process it asynchronously. But an HR rep confirming an employee's current department while a case is open and waiting needs request-response, because a real person is waiting right now. Matching the pattern to the actual need is the judgment call, not picking one pattern for everything.

Security has to hold the same balance. Some data here is genuinely regulated — health-related leave cases, facilities tied to patient-care units — and that deserves strict, audited access. But locking the entire platform down at that level would push Lakeshore and Prairie View staff toward exactly what Chapter 5 warned about: shared logins or a shadow tracker outside ServiceNow. So strict controls stay narrow, on the tables that actually need them, and everything else stays fast.

These three decisions aren't independent — domain tagging has to be correct on every incoming HR record, and the corporate domain, where data crosses hospital boundaries, is exactly where the tightest security matters most. Next, we turn all of this into a real architecture deliverable and a written decision record.
